# Sea-star wasting in Southern California: was the cascade response driven by sunflower-star loss?

*Generated by `code/R/20_compound_disturbance.R`. Tests whether the 2013–14 sea-star
wasting disease (SSWD) — a different stressor type from the marine heatwave — drove
the MPA cascade response, as a complement to the heat-only framing of Kumagai (2024)
and the disease-focused Eisaguirre (2020). **This version corrects an earlier draft
that conflated the wrong sea-star species and ignored the patchiness of the sunflower
star; the corrected conclusion is the opposite of the draft's.***

---

## The species and distribution problem (why the first attempt was wrong)
SSWD killed >20 sea-star species, but only the **sunflower star (*Pycnopodia
helianthoides*)** is a major urchin predator — and it is a **cold-water** species. In
the Southern California Bight it was **patchy**:

- It made up only **~9% of the large sea-star density** in our region; the rest was
  *Pisaster giganteus*, which dominated the counts but eats snails/bivalves, **not a
  primary urchin predator**. An earlier draft lumped the two and reported a "99%
  sea-star crash" — that crash was mostly *Pisaster*.
- Pre-SSWD (2008–2012), only **8 of 30 SoCal reserves** had meaningful sunflower star
  (≥0.5 per 60 m²) — the colder, northern/island reefs (Harris Point, Naples, Painted
  Cave, South Point, Begg Rock, Point Conception, Gull Island, Campus Point). The
  other **~2/3 had essentially none** (Anacapa SMRs, Catalina sites, southern
  mainland; Fig. a). Mean Pycnopodia was 1.0 per 60 m² in the north vs 0.25 in the
  south.

So at most SoCal reserves **there was no sunflower star to lose** — a uniform
"keystone-predator-removal" framing does not apply.

## The test: does the cascade response scale with sunflower-star loss?
Because pre-SSWD sunflower-star abundance *varies* among reserves while the 2014–16
heatwave hit them all, we can partly separate the two: if the cascade reorganization
is stronger where more sunflower star was lost, that is an SSWD signal beyond the
heatwave. We compared the after-vs-before change in the MPA effect (lnRR) between
reserves that **had** sunflower stars and those that had **~none**
(`table_compound_keystone_moderation.csv`):

| Taxon | had sunflower stars (k=5) | ~none (k=6) | period × group interaction |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Giant kelp** | +1.50 (p=0.001) | **+1.57 (p=0.025)** | −0.23, **p=0.78 (n.s.)** |
| Purple urchin | −0.40 (n.s.) | −0.77 (n.s.) | −0.14, p=0.85 (n.s.) |
| Red urchin | −0.19 (n.s.) | −0.27 (n.s.) | +0.24, p=0.70 (n.s.) |

**The kelp recovery and urchin decline are statistically indistinguishable — and the
point estimates nearly identical — whether or not a reserve ever had sunflower
stars.** There is no evidence that sunflower-star loss drove the cascade response.

## Corrected conclusion
In the Southern California Bight, **the MPA cascade resilience is attributable to the
marine heatwave plus fishing protection, not to sea-star wasting.** The kelp increase
inside reserves through 2013–2016 is real and robust (and repeats across two
heatwaves, script 19), but it occurs **equally at reserves that never had a sunflower
star**, so it cannot be a sunflower-star compensation effect. The keystone-removal /
trophic-redundancy mechanism that Eisaguirre (2020) documented at the **cold-water
Northern Channel Islands**, where sunflower stars were abundant, **does not generalize
to most of our warmer system** because the disease's keystone target was largely
absent here.

This is actually a cleaner result than the flawed draft: it removes a potential
confound and **strengthens the heatwave-resilience interpretation** (aligning with
Kumagai 2024 and our scripts 14 & 19) — the kelp recovery is not a sea-star artifact.
It also sharpens the scope statement: a genuine SSWD-resilience test requires the
cold-water reefs that actually had sunflower stars (Eisaguirre's NCI), and SoCal
should **not** be framed as a compound SSWD + MHW system for the cascade.

## Cross-study synthesis (`table_compound_crossstudy.csv`)
| Study | Region | Disturbance | Sunflower star | Inference |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Eisaguirre 2020 | W. N. Channel Islands (cold) | SSWD | abundant → strong keystone loss | protected predators compensate for sunflower-star loss |
| Kumagai 2024 | S. + Central CA | 2014–16 MHW | context only | MPAs preserve cascade → kelp heat resilience |
| **This study** | **S. California Bight** | MHW (SSWD target mostly absent) | **patchy: ~1/3 of reserves** | **kelp resilience is heat + protection, not sunflower-star loss** |

## Caveats
- Moderation power is limited (5 high- vs 6 low-Pycnopodia reserves per taxon); but
  the point estimates are nearly equal (not merely non-significant), which is stronger
  evidence of "no keystone effect" than a power-limited null alone.
- We cannot fully exclude a minor urchin-predation role for *Pisaster*, or sub-lethal
  effects; and SSWD/MHW remain temporally confounded at the few reefs that did have
  sunflower stars.
- Southern California only.

## Reproducibility
`code/R/20_compound_disturbance.R` (standalone; reads raw PISCO swath for the
sunflower-star distribution, skips that section if absent). Outputs:
`tables/table_compound_pycnopodia_distribution.csv`,
`table_compound_pycnopodia_crash.csv`, `table_compound_keystone_moderation.csv`,
`table_compound_resilience.csv`, `table_compound_crossstudy.csv`,
`plots/fig_compound_disturbance.{pdf,png}`.

### Figure legend
**Figure S — Sea-star wasting and the MPA cascade in Southern California.** (a)
Pre-SSWD (2008–2012) sunflower-star (*Pycnopodia*) density per reserve (log axis);
blue = reserves that had sunflower stars (≥0.5 per 60 m²), orange = ~none. The
sunflower star was present at only ~1/3 of reserves (cold/northern/island) and
essentially absent at the rest. (b) After-vs-before change in the MPA effect (lnRR)
for kelp and urchins, split by whether a reserve had sunflower stars; the responses
are indistinguishable between groups, indicating the cascade response is not driven
by sunflower-star loss.
